messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh's Vigil

Rajesh was seventy-five when he finally agreed to see a therapist, though his wife Priya had been asking for two years. He had come to America in 1972 as a young man, carrying little more than the skills his grandfather had taught him—how to center clay, how to feel the wall thin beneath his thumbs, how to coax water and earth into vessels that held things. For fifty years he had made pots in his small studio in Queens, and the work had sustained him through everything: raising two children, the death of his parents, the slow forgetting that comes with age. But in the past three years, something had shifted. The studio felt unsafe now. His hands, which had always known what to do, had begun to shake.

It had started with a phone call in the spring of 2021. His cousin Arun had been killed in a car accident in Dhaka—struck by a taxi while crossing a street. The funeral was held in absentia; Rajesh could not travel. When the news came, something had cracked open in him, and with it came a flood of images he had spent five decades learning not to see.

He had been sixteen when the partition came. He lived in what became East Pakistan, in a neighborhood where Hindu and Muslim families had lived side by side for generations. In March of 1971, soldiers arrived. He remembered the sound first—not gunfire, but the grinding of truck engines, the metallic slam of doors, voices shouting in a language that was his own but had become the language of threat. He had hidden in his mother's storage room while soldiers moved through the house. They had taken his older brother. Rajesh had heard the sounds—the rough handling, his brother's voice calling out—but could not see. The not-seeing had somehow made it worse. For weeks afterward, he could not assemble what had happened into a coherent narrative. The images came in fragments: a boot, a shadow across the doorway, his mother's hand gripping his shoulder so hard it left bruises. He had never been able to speak about it in a way that made sense, even to himself.

He had left Pakistan in 1972, and America had given him clay and silence. For decades, he had not thought about it. Then Arun died in a car accident, and suddenly the sound of engines—the particular grinding roar of heavy vehicles—became unbearable. When a police car passed his studio with its siren on, his heart would race so violently he thought he might collapse. Funerals were impossible now. His daughter had married last year, and he had sat in the back pew unable to fully breathe, convinced that something terrible was about to happen.

Rajesh had begun to change his life in ways that made no sense even to him. He stopped attending community events. When his grandson was born, he had felt a surge of joy so intense and so immediately followed by dread—what if something happened to the boy, what if he could not protect him—that he had made excuses not to visit. His wife had wept. He knew he was wrong to withdraw from his own grandchild, but the alternative felt impossible: to hope was to invite catastrophe.

At the studio, he found himself scanning the street constantly, watching for police cars, listening for the sound of heavy engines. His concentration shattered. A pot that should have taken an hour now took three, because his hands would not obey. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the one thing that had made him himself. At night, he lay beside Priya, who had loved him for fifty-three years, and he could not tell her that he was terrified. Not of dying—he was old, death was reasonable—but of the feeling that at any moment, without warning, the world could splinter again.

When Priya finally insisted, he came to the appointment. He sat in the chair across from the therapist and said very little. But when asked about the worst moment, he closed his eyes and spoke of a sound—not words, but the memory of a sound—and his hands began to shake again, as if his body remembered what his mind had never quite assembled into language.
